items.title: Counterfactual Profile Perturbations for Recommendation Explanations: A Reproducibility Study
items.content: arXiv:2610.36208v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This reproducibility paper explores the counterfactual explanation technique known as Learning to eXplain Recommendations (LXR). Prior work has shown that LXR can reliably identify perturbations that, if applied to a user's profile, cause the user's top ranked item to no longer be recommended, thereby explaining the item's recommendation as a function of the user's rating choices. In this paper, we extend this work in multiple ways. We expand the scope of the original LXR study to look at explanations for items other than the most highly recommended item, finding that LXR is also effective at this version of the task. We consider alternate baselines for LXR, including item popularity and latent factor similarity, and we see that for some tasks these alternatives work surprisingly well. We also examine the impact of item popularity, finding that LXR offers better explanation quality (shorter perturbations) when less popular items are being explained. Finally, we conduct a brute-force exploration of a subset of the perturbation space in order to estimate a lower bound for optimal perturbation size against which LXR and other such methods can be compared.
items.author: Meysam Varasteh, Elizabeth McKinnie, Robin Burke
items.summary: This reproducibility study extends the LXR technique for counterfactual recommendation explanations, testing whether it works for explaining items other than the top-ranked one and comparing against alternative baselines like item popularity and latent factor similarity. The findings confirm effectiveness for the extended task while revealing nuances where some baselines are competitive. Reproducibility work of this kind strengthens the evidentiary base for explainable recommendation.
items.reasoning: Valuable rigor and honest baseline comparisons, but as a reproducibility and extension of an existing technique its novelty and headline impact are inherently modest. Useful for the recommender-systems explainability community.

items.title: Tap2Listen: Instant Target Switching for Streaming Audio-Visual Speaker Extraction
items.content: arXiv:2610.36643v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AV-TSE) uses a target speaker's face to extract the speaker's speech from an input audio mixture in real time. However, existing systems fix the target speaker for an entire clip, while conversation demands frequent and immediate target switches. To address this problem, we propose Tap2Listen, a streaming AV-TSE model designed for instant response to target switches. The model separates computation by modality: the target-agnostic audio encoder processes only the mixture, while the target-specific visual cues of the selected face condition only the decoder. A switch requires only a 0.12ms re-projection and takes effect immediately. We also design component-wise losses: a prediction loss for the encoder and a supervised extraction loss for the decoder. For evaluation, we measure how quickly output quality recovers after a switch. On the standard LRS3-2mix test set, Tap2Listen improves SI-SNRi from 8.85 to 9.68 dB at a comparable parameter count. After a switch to a known face, the model produces full-quality output from the first frame, whereas the baseline needs about 1 second to recover. Finally, we show that the proposed streaming AV-TSE model runs in real time on a single CPU core.

items.title: Developing a Speech Language Model for Basque
items.content: arXiv:2610.36911v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.

Data scarcity is addressed by translating VoiceAssistant-400K into Basque and synthesizing audio with a Basque TTS, achieving reasonable content quality and intelligibility scores.

items.title: What the Primary Lund Plane Omits: A Model-Stitching Diagnosis of a Jet-Tagger Representation Gap
items.content: arXiv:2610.37137v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Lund-plane and Particle Transformer (ParT) jet taggers can differ in performance because one representation is weaker, or because a weaker downstream computation reads an adequate one. Standalone performance cannot separate these. Model stitching can: it links the frozen early layers of one network to the frozen late layers of another through a single trained linear map. As a positive control we use an incomplete Lund representation, the primary declustering branch, whose deficit is known independently. Stitched into ParT's downstream, it reaches a background rejection at least as much as its own downstream recovers, yet far below ParT's background rejection: the deficit is representational, not computational. A hypergraph reader over splitting triplets does no better, ruling out higher-order correlations as the cause. The gap is invisible in AUC, which stays within 1\% of its target value, and appears only in background rejection at low signal efficiency. It localizes to 0.6\% of background jets, at and above the top mass, with more constituents but fewer primary splittings than typical background. Rebuilding the representation on the full Cambridge/Aachen declustering tree repairs the deficit as predicted: standalone rejection rises, closing 72\% of the gap. Masking nodes at inference shows the repaired network still relies almost entirely on the primary branch; the secondary splittings make the representation learnable rather than supplying information it reads. Along the primary branch, the widest-angle splitting, near the top and $W$ opening angles, is worth nearly twice a random one. For quark/gluon tagging the primary branch is far less deficient, retaining 77.6\% of ParT's rejection (46.9\% for top), and the full tree closes only 33\% of the gap (72\% for top).

The methodology offers a clean attribution tool for physics ML architectures.

items.title: HGPRGDel: GPR-Aware Learning and Ranking for Growth-Coupled Gene Deletion Design
items.content: arXiv:2610.37478v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, in which cellular growth is linked to the synthesis of a target compound through genetic interventions, is a fundamental goal in metabolic engineering. Constraint-based methods can identify growth-coupled deletion strategies, but design for each target typically requires a separate search across a large number of possible gene-deletion combinations. This motivates a reusable approach that learns from previously evaluated strain designs to prioritize candidate interventions before downstream constraint-based evaluation. We present a reproducible protocol for growth-coupled gene deletion design that learns and ranks gene-deletion priorities for each target metabolite. Using computationally curated deletion strategies as learning resources, the protocol generates continuous deletion-priority rankings, constructs candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates these candidates through constraint-based metabolic analysis. Its learning component, HGPRGDel, explicitly represents gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes can jointly support a reaction or alternative genes can maintain its activity, while integrating molecular and reaction-level information. Across e_coli_core, iMM904, and iML1515, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among the evaluated learning configurations. HGPRGDel's rankings recovered an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from MetNetComp by examining fewer genes than the evaluated baseline methods. By separating learned intervention prioritization from downstream constraint-based assessment, the protocol provides a reproducible framework for reusing strain-design knowledge while controlling the size of the candidate space and retaining mechanistic evaluation of growth-coupled production.

items.title: Some different lenses of agency and their implications for alignment
items.content:
TL;DR; These nine lenses on agency give you a wide range of tools to model and interpret agents. Each gives you lens-specific alignment methods and lens-specific risks to address.

Epistemic status: Little here is new in a general sense; it's value lies in the synthesis and in providing a single point of reference.

The concepts of agent and agency (derived from the Latin agere, to do or drive) are ubiquitous in AI safety, yet they do not pick out a clearly bounded set of things or properties and are used in a great variety of ways. 

One response to this is to argue about their ‘proper’ use (e.g. what is a ‘real’ agent). However, we suggest that because of these terms’ centrality to how we think about both humans and AI systems, it may be better to survey this diversity as offering various ‘lenses’ through which the fundamental challenges of alignment can be perceived. 

Below, we describe a varied assortment of these lenses, what they tend to highlight and obscure, and how they influence the way we think about AI risk and alignment. This list, and the framing behind it, comes out of discussions at the 2026 PIBBSS summer fellowship.

## Agents as goal-directed systems

Many formal definitions of agency are based on the concept of agents as (better or worse approximations of) goal directed systems. The concept of a goal can itself be understood in different ways, meaning this definition doesn’t always cohere with its most everyday reading. However, it focuses on modeling agents’ behaviour, for instance using tools from decision theory, game theory, and related fields....
items.author: SJ_Beard
items.summary: A conceptual survey presenting nine lenses on agency (e.g., agents as goal-directed systems) drawn from 2026 PIBBSS fellowship discussions, describing what each lens highlights and obscures and the alignment methods and risks each implies. The author is explicit that the value is synthesis and providing a single reference point rather than new results.
items.reasoning: A useful taxonomy for AI safety conceptual work: organizing diverse usages of agency into lenses with per-lens alignment implications could help researchers notice blind spots. It is honest about containing little that is new, lacks formal or empirical contribution, and its impact depends on uptake, but synthesis work of this kind has real value in the field.

The concepts of agent and agency (derived from the Latin agere, to do or drive) are ubiquitous in AI safety, yet they do not pick out a clearly bounded set of things or properties and are used in a great variety of ways.

One response to this is to argue about their ‘proper’ use (e.g. what is a ‘real’ agent). However, we suggest that because of these terms’ centrality to how we think about both humans and AI systems, it may be better to survey this diversity as offering various ‘lenses’ through which the fundamental challenges of alignment can be perceived.

Below, we describe a varied assortment of these lenses, what they tend to highlight and obscure, and how they influence the way we think about AI risk and alignment. This list, and the framing behind it, comes out of discussions at the 2026 PIBBSS summer fellowship.

Agents as goal-directed systems

Many formal definitions of agency are based on the concept of agents as (better or worse approximations of) goal directed systems. The concept of a goal can itself be understood in different ways, meaning this definition doesn’t always cohere with its most everyday reading. However, it focuses on modeling agents’ behaviour, for instance using tools from decision theory, game theory, and related fields....

items.title: Learning Where to Trust: Reliability-Guided Expert Routing and Velocity Gating for 3D Deformable Registration
items.content: arXiv:2610.36672v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deformable image registration relies on accurate anatomical correspondences. However, explicitly coupling local matching reliability with spatial context selection and deformation update strength remains insufficiently explored in learning-based registration. This challenge is particularly pronounced in homogeneous, weakly textured, and severely deformed regions, where ambiguous matches may induce erroneous deformation updates. We propose ReliMorph, a reliability-routed symmetric framework for 3D deformable registration that couples correspondence assessment with spatial context selection and update strength.Local correlation distributions characterize correspondence ambiguity using shared anatomical features with modality-specific adaptation. These reliability cues guide spatial expert fusion and gate residual velocities during coarse-to-fine refinement. Updated inverse-inconsistency feedback guides routing and gating at finer pyramid levels. To our knowledge, ReliMorph is the first 3D deformable registration framework to jointly condition spatial expert routing and residual velocity gating on correspondence reliability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReliMorph consistently outperforms competing methods in anatomical overlap, highlighting its effectiveness across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.

items.title: Do bots feel bad? Assessing empirical evidence for functional valence in LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2610.36962v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Do LLMs have valenced states, i.e. states that feel pleasant or unpleasant? Recent empirical work has claimed to show that LLMs possess functional valenced states (e.g. ``functional pleasure and pain'' [Ren et al. 2026], ``functional emotions'' [Sofroniew et al. 2026], and ``functional welfare'' [Han et al. 2026]) that play the same causal role as valenced states in cognition and action, without necessarily being consciously experienced. But it remains unexplored how well the identified states fit the functional role of valence as understood in the philosophical and cognitive science literature. Here, I assess the current body of evidence, and argue (i) that key aspects of valence remain untested in LLMs, and (ii) that extant empirical paradigms inadequately distinguish (functional) valence from neighbouring constructs like preferences, value-judgments, valence attributions and role-play. I conclude by sketching some novel experimental approaches to better target (functional) valence itself.
items.author: Iwan Williams
items.summary: This philosophical analysis critically assesses recent empirical claims that LLMs possess functional valenced states such as functional pleasure, pain, emotions, and welfare. The author argues that key aspects of valence, as understood in philosophy and cognitive science, remain untested in LLMs and that existing experimental paradigms are inadequate for the functional role.
items.reasoning: A timely and rigorous philosophical critique of an emerging empirical literature on LLM welfare, relevant to AI safety discourse. Its importance is somewhat bounded by being an evaluative commentary rather than new empirical or methodological work, but it usefully raises evidential standards.

items.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Algorithmic Resilience and the Non-Linear Governance Premium in Sovereign Capital Flows
items.content: arXiv:2610.35895v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Despite the proliferation of sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) metrics, traditional linear macro-financial models systematically misprice Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) tail risks during systemic shocks. This paper demonstrates that sovereign risk transmission is fundamentally non-linear. Using a forward-chained global panel of 147 sovereign entities (2010-2024), we deploy a gradient boosting architecture that compresses forecast errors by over 39% against L1-regularized baselines precisely during extreme macroeconomic tail events. Moving beyond opaque predictive accuracy, we apply dual interpretability frameworks to mathematically map the discrete threshold effects of institutional quality. We identify a strict, non-linear "Governance Premium": incremental environmental and social improvements yield zero capital advantage until a foundational regulatory threshold is breached. Finally, we establish regime-conditional 95% uncertainty bounds that maintain valid marginal coverage even under severe ESG reporting failures. This framework equips policymakers with a distribution-free tool to quantify sovereign tail-risk, proving that global capital markets price institutional resilience as a discrete boundary rather than a continuous premium.

items.title: Dirichlet Process Mixtures within Semiparametric Bayesian Networks: A Novel Conditional Density Estimation Approach
items.content: arXiv:2610.36110v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBNs) are flexible probabilistic graphical models for representing joint distributions of continuous variables through lower-dimensional conditional probability distributions (CPDs). Existing SPBN models use kernel density estimators (KDEs) for non-parametric CPD modeling, but their one-component-per-observation mixture representation can lead to increased inference costs and density estimation errors, which can be limiting. In this work, we define a new CPD modeling approach for non-parametric components based on Bayesian non-parametric Dirichlet Process Mixtures (DPMs) within SPBNs. DPMs provide a data-adaptive clustering of observations, yielding a more compact representation while retaining the flexibility of non-parametric density estimation, unlike KDE. This results in lower inference costs while improving density estimation performance. We implement the proposed DPM-based SPBN (DPM-SPBN) by extending the open-source PyBNesian package and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world data. For a given network structure, DPM-based CPDs significantly outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian network models for continuous variables in density estimation, achieving lower absolute log-likelihood errors on synthetic data. We further investigate the impact of the proposed CPD modeling on structure learning methods relying on CPD-based scores. DPM-based SPBNs achieve lower structure learning and density estimation errors than KDE-based SPBNs. Experiments on real-world data corroborate these findings, identifying DPM-based CPD modeling as the most effective alternative among the evaluated non-parametric approaches for continuous variables.

items.summary: This paper replaces kernel density estimators for non-parametric conditional distributions in semiparametric Bayesian networks with Dirichlet Process Mixtures, yielding a data-adaptive, more compact mixture representation. The DPM-based CPD modeling aims to reduce inference costs and density estimation errors relative to one-component-per-observation KDEs.
items.reasoning: A principled Bayesian nonparametric contribution that plausibly improves the scalability of semiparametric graphical models, from a credible academic group in machine learning. However, it is a methodological refinement within a classic (non-deep) modeling family with limited apparent connection to current frontier AI research, so impact is likely confined to the Bayesian ML community.

items.title: AI-Assisted Discovery of CNOT Decompositions for Quantum Permutations on Constrained Topologies
items.content: arXiv:2610.37045v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Efficient quantum circuit compilation is challenging for quantum computers, where limited qubit connectivity can introduce substantial overhead in the implementation of logical operations. Recent AI-assisted synthesis methods have shown considerable potential for reducing circuit complexity, but their role in uncovering principles that can guide the design of new deterministic compilation algorithms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate this perspective for the synthesis of quantum permutations into CNOT circuits under constrained qubit connectivity. Using AlphaCNOT as an exploratory tool, we identify a recurring decomposition for remote transpositions that improves on the construction based on adjacent SWAP routing. For two qubits at graph distance $d>1$, the discovered pattern yields a topology-legal implementation using at most $6d-4$ CNOT gates, compared to the $6d-3$ gates required by the corresponding SWAP-based construction. We formalize this observation through a constructive proof to define Global Transpositions, a deterministic synthesis method that searches for a minimum-cost decomposition of an entire permutation into topology-aware logical transpositions. The resulting method subsumes optimal SWAP routing within its synthesis model and provides certified upper bounds on the topology-constrained CNOT cost. Our experiments also reveal circuits that cannot be expressed as concatenations of independently synthesized transpositions. Instead, these circuits exploit intermediate linear transformations that temporarily leave the permutation subgroup and combine partial effects of multiple logical operations, a mechanism we call intermediate CNOT fusion. Our results show that AI-assisted synthesis can support not only circuit optimization, but also the discovery of reusable identities, provable constructions, and hidden mechanisms in quantum circuit compilation.

items.title: A Smart Instant Book Filter Model based on Dual-Objective Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.36287v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hospitality service in online marketplaces has become increasingly popular over the past few years, not only because it helps people easily rent short-term lodging but also because it empowers travelers to connect with locals and feel belonging. A typical pattern of these industries is a central platform mediating the economic interactions between guests and hosts, where a successful booking experience is the key to user satisfaction. However, one of the biggest challenges is the possible delay of response and chance of rejection when guests try to book a request-to-book listing. Previously, we enabled the instant book feature to allow hosts to instantly accept qualified guests and guests to confirm bookings immediately. Yet the symptom has not been alleviated given mixed request-to-book and instant book listing supply in search results. One possible solution is to promote all instant book listings in search results; however, booking rate will be damaged due to some improperly promoted low quality listings.   In this paper, we present a novel smart instant book filter system that applies the instant book filter intelligently and shifts request-to-book to instant book without hurting booking rate. Compared with traditional two-sided markets research that targets finding strategies to maximize a single overall social welfare goal, our proposed system aims to maximize the instant book rate with the constraint that booking rate should not decrease, forming a dual-objective optimization problem.   We show A/B testing results for our system exposed to global users, demonstrating that our model performs better than previous human-expert-tuned models in terms of both instant book rate and overall booking rate. We also achieved improved metrics such as the host instant book adoption rate. The proposed system has been deployed to production and is serving millions of users every day.

items.summary: This paper presents a dual-objective optimization model for deciding which booking requests to auto-accept via instant book in hospitality marketplaces, addressing response delays and rejections on request-to-book listings. It extends a previously deployed instant-book feature with a smarter filter to improve booking outcomes for guests and hosts. The work is a concrete industrial application of ML to marketplace trust and conversion.

items.title: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2610.36625v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.

items.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.36888v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FAST.Farm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.

A low-fidelity acoustic model enables training at reduced computational cost.
items.reasoning: A solid applied RL contribution with clear industrial relevance, jointly handling a coupling (wake and acoustics) that prior noise mitigation ignored. However, it is a domain-specific application of standard model-free RL methods with limited broader AI-methodological novelty.

items.title: Multiple Leak Localization in Water Distribution Networks through Graph Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.35972v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Leak localization in water distribution networks is challenging when multiple leaks occur simultaneously, particularly under sparse monitoring. Existing data-driven methods often assume a single or predefined number of leaks or require extensive enumeration of leak combinations. This study proposes a graph neural network (GNN) model that localizes a variable number of simultaneous leaks without specifying the leak count in advance or exhaustively generating every possible combination of leak locations for training. The model is evaluated on two benchmark networks of different sizes, the 31-node Hanoi network and the larger 92-node NET3 network, under variable demand, sparse pressure-sensor coverage, variable leak magnitudes, and varying numbers of simultaneous leaks. The GNN outperforms multilayer perceptron, support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, and random forest classifiers by up to 12% and 20% in accuracy respectively in Hanoi and NET3 networks. Consistent performance across both networks supports the scalability of the proposed approach.
items.author: Arvin Ajoodani, Sara Nazif, Pouria Ramazi
items.summary: This paper proposes a GNN model that localizes a variable number of simultaneous leaks in water distribution networks without pre-specifying the leak count or exhaustively enumerating leak combinations during training. It is evaluated on the 31-node Hanoi and 92-node NET3 benchmark networks under sparse sensing and variable demand.
items.reasoning: A useful applied contribution with a practical formulation (variable-count localization under sparse monitoring), but small benchmark networks, an academic author team, and limited generalization evidence constrain its significance to the broader AI field.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.35972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Leak localization in water distribution networks is challenging when multiple leaks occur simultaneously, particularly under sparse monitoring. Existing data-driven methods often assume a single or predefined number of leaks or require extensive enumeration of leak combinations. This study proposes a graph neural network (GNN) model that localizes a variable number of simultaneous leaks without specifying the leak count in advance or exhaustively generating every possible combination of leak locations for training. The model is evaluated on two benchmark networks of different sizes, the 31-node Hanoi network and the larger 92-node NET3 network, under variable demand, sparse pressure-sensor coverage, variable leak magnitudes, and varying numbers of simultaneous leaks. The GNN outperforms multilayer perceptron, support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, and random forest classifiers by up to 12% and 20% in accuracy respectively in Hanoi and NET3 networks. Consistent performance across both networks supports the scalability of the proposed approach.

items.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
items.content: arXiv:2610.36583v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.

items.title: An Algebra of Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2610.36795v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: On the theoretic analyses on transforms, they mainly focus on the computability analysis, such the Turing-completeness of unbounded precision transformers, the advantage of parallelizability of unbounded precision transformers and the limitations of bounded precision transformers. This paper give transformers an algebra for reasoning, which relies heavily on the functional decomposition results of transformers. This algebra uses functional decompositions as atomic actions, includes sequential composition and parallel composition, recursion for feedback and abstraction for hidden layers. As we know, it is the first attempt to model transformers logically and can be used to verify the correctness of transformer based applications.
items.author: Yong Wang, Zhiyan Wang, Hexiao Kang
items.summary: This theoretical paper builds an algebra for reasoning about transformers, using functional decompositions as atomic actions with sequential and parallel composition, recursion, and abstraction. The authors claim it is the first attempt to model transformers logically and that it enables correctness verification of transformer-based applications.
items.reasoning: Formal reasoning about transformers is a worthwhile goal, and the claimed first-mover algebraic framing is interesting. However, the abstract is short on demonstrated results or verified applications, and the practical payoff of such algebras is often limited, so the score reflects promise over proven impact.

items.title: What do we mean by ‘long-horizon’ work?
items.content:
TL;DR - The benchmarks frontier labs cite for long-horizon capability mostly measure capability on tasks involving many steps or lots of context, verifiable end states, and little external input. I argue that what defines real-world long-horizon work is delayed external feedback. That delay is where human input becomes high leverage, and it’s a constraint neither longer context nor multi-agent swarms can engineer away. I discuss this with examples like building a new, better Redis vs. running personalized lead conversion campaigns.

Earlier this month, while working on task design for scalable oversight-related problem statements, my teammates at Lossfunk and I disagreed on what are good examples of long-horizon work. I suggested “run personalized digital lead conversion campaigns,” while my more software-minded teammates recommended, “build a better and different Redis.”

This got me reading about how to define long-horizon tasks, and as it turns out, we weren't alone in our confusion.

Investor and Operator Nikunj Kothari tweeting about how ‘long horizon’ is a concept he has heard highly varied and wildly different definitions for.

I figured the best way to resolve this confusion was to review recent model release reports and note how frontier model labs talk about the concept and the benchmarks they use to report capabilities on this front. I also reviewed additional papers I found on arXiv. My current main takeaways from my reading are:...

items.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.36991v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.
items.author: Zafer Sahinoglu, Abdulazeez Mohammed, Buse Yaren Kazangirler, Cahit Berkay Kazangirler
items.summary: SpectRAG combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection to improve multi-hop RAG. By representing chunks with both dense embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates, it mitigates redundancy, missed cross-chunk dependencies, and incomplete evidence in independently ranked dense retrieval.
items.reasoning: A competent systems contribution combining several known techniques (graphs, spectral methods, budgeted selection) into a coherent RAG pipeline for multi-hop queries. The assembly is sensible but largely incremental; without strong empirical evidence visible, impact appears moderate.

items.title: Enhancing Deep Learning Model Performance through Data Generation Strategies: Classification of Olive Tree Diseases
items.content: arXiv:2610.35984v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deep learning models are highly effective in a wide range of domains, particu larly in plant disease diagnosis. However, their performance is often limited by challenges such as insufficient data and class imbalance. In our work, we propose a comprehensive data generation strategy to overcome these limitations. First, we apply various data generation techniques, including traditional augmentation methods, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic image generation using Deep Convolu tional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), to create new data samples. Second, we exploit this generated data in three scenarios: (S1) balancing class distribution in the original dataset, (S2) increasing the number of samples per class, and (S3) expanding the dataset while maintaining balanced classes. Third, we evaluate the impact of these data distributions (S1, S2, S3) on model perfor mance using the EfficientNetV2B0 architecture with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights. The experimental results show a substantial improvement in classifica tion accuracy, emphasizing the critical role of data diversity and class balance. These findings highlight the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed strat egy of data generation and distribution for enhancing dataset quality, offering promising applications in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.
items.author: Hicham El Akhal, Abderrahim Waga, Aissa Ben Yahya, Abdelbaki El Belrhiti El Alaoui
items.summary: The paper applies a suite of data generation techniques including CutMix, MixUp, and DCGAN-based synthetic images to address data scarcity and class imbalance in olive tree disease classification. It evaluates three scenarios for using generated data: balancing classes, increasing per-class samples, and expanding the dataset overall. The work targets a practically important agricultural diagnosis problem with limited data.
items.reasoning: Solid applied work on a domain-relevant problem, but the techniques (augmentation plus DCGANs) are well-established rather than novel. Novelty and general methodological impact are modest; value is mainly for the agricultural vision community.

items.title: Dependency Graphs of Mathematical Arguments: Representation, Structural Measurement, and Proof Review
items.content: arXiv:2610.36776v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose a source-grounded framework for representing and measuring mathematical arguments with assistance from large language models. It includes numbered and unnumbered statements, equations, assumptions, and constructions, distinguishing source occurrences from contextual states and inference records. Proposed dependencies retain source evidence and review status. A measurement contract fixes manuscript versions, boundaries, granularity, proof choices, and macro anchors. On a selected finite directed acyclic graph, depth is the longest prerequisite-path length, and bulk counts distinct ancestor edges. We give a union recurrence that accounts for shared subarguments and identify reachability conditions preserving depth and the macro skeleton; unrestricted refinement need not preserve depth or bulk. A standardized, versioned prompt protocol separates annotation discovery, deterministic recomputation, and review assistance. Cross-paper links support a research agenda on theorem co-use, rare combinations, and connections between dependency communities. These patterns motivate probabilistic premise suggestions and review of possible omissions or unchecked application conditions in human-written and AI-generated proofs. Further applications include source-linked reading support and comparison of individual and collaborative argument shapes. We provide an evaluation design rather than empirical evidence of these benefits. Suggested premises require mathematical validation, and the measures describe a specified representation rather than intrinsic mathematical difficulty, originality, or importance.

items.reasoning: A thoughtful formalization effort at the intersection of LLM-assisted mathematics and proof verification, but it is primarily a representation framework with limited empirical validation, and its adoption depends on community uptake of the representation contract.

items.title: Structured Time-Frequency Representation for Channel Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.35956v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate CSI forecasting is essential for mitigating channel aging and supporting reliable downlink transmission in high-mobility wireless systems. In FDD systems, forecasting future DL CSI from historical UL observations requires joint temporal extrapolation and cross-band inference. However, defining historical UL as the input and future DL as the target does not specify how elapsed time and UL-to-DL band separation should be represented in a pretrained predictor's positional space. FAR-CSI establishes an FDD-aware representation of channel forecasting within a joint temporal and operating-band positional field. Within this field, historical UL observations and future DL targets occupy segregated regions according to their temporal and operating-band roles, preserving the distinction between observed UL context and unobserved DL prediction targets. This representation is instantiated through a unified structured routing rule that governs encoder positional assignment, decoder-field reconstruction, and future-DL target selection, ensuring the same FDD geometry is preserved from contextual encoding to prediction readout. Under matched backbone, initialization, and training conditions, FDD-aware routing reduces NMSE by 21.44\% relative to generic routing. Across the evaluated FDD baselines, FAR-CSI achieves higher CSI prediction accuracy and MRT-based spectral efficiency, while retaining its predictive advantage across mobility conditions, prediction horizons, reduced training-data regimes, and noisy historical observations.
items.author: Ning Yang, Yuming Xian, Tong Li, Ning Gao, Haijun Zhang
items.summary: FAR-CSI is an FDD-aware representation for wireless channel state information forecasting that places historical uplink observations and future downlink targets in segregated regions of a joint temporal and operating-band positional field. This addresses how elapsed time and UL-to-DL band separation should be encoded in pretrained predictors for high-mobility systems.
items.reasoning: A specialized wireless communications contribution with a sensible representational insight, but it sits outside core AI research themes, and the abstract alone provides limited evidence of broad impact or evaluation rigor.

items.title: Interview with James Mattingly on Machine Agency (coauthored with Beba Cibralic)
items.content:
Crossposted on X here: https://x.com/kevin__dong__/status/2115079682412728352

On October 20, 2026, Kevin Dong conducted an interview with James Mattingly, Professor of Philosophy at Georgetown University and coauthor of Machine Agency (2025) with Beba Cibralic. What follows is a lightly edited transcript of their conversation.

https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262549981/machine-agency/

James Mattingly: Neither Beba Cibralic nor I are particularly experts in AI. We come at it from very different directions, both from each other and from perspectives that aren’t primarily about artificial intelligence. She comes at it more or less from just war theory. She was a graduate student at Georgetown whom I recruited around 2016 or 2017, and she was doing a PhD in political philosophy.

One of the things we do at Georgetown, like every graduate program, is have these gatekeeping courses. One of them is in logic, which I frequently teach to graduate students. I teach the course from the perspective of computability, using Boolos, Burgess, and Jeffrey’s Computability and Logic. So a lot of the fundamental results concerning incompleteness, representability, and so forth are presented from the perspective of Turing-machine implementation and the equivalence between Turing machines and other kinds of machines.

In the spring of 2020, Beba and another graduate student asked me to teach a graduate seminar on the philosophy of technology, which I knew a little about, but not much. So we had to start from scratch, and we worked it up together. A lot of different things came up, but one recurring question was who was responsible for decisions made by the AI systems being used at the time for loan approvals, various background checks, and so forth. Banks were rolling these systems out, and they were completely inscrutable. Nobody knew exactly what was going on inside them....

items.summary: A lightly edited October 2026 interview by Kevin Dong with philosopher James Mattingly, coauthor of the 2025 MIT Press book Machine Agency with Beba Cibralic. The discussion covers their non-AI-specialist perspectives, including just war theory and computability theory, as lenses on questions of machine agency.
items.reasoning: A substantive philosophical interview relevant to AI agency and governance debates, but it is a transcript and commentary rather than original research. The cross-disciplinary angle from an academic philosopher adds some value for AI-safety-adjacent conceptual work.

items.title: scPyviewer: a Python-native interactive viewer from AnnData single-cell data
items.content: arXiv:2610.35890v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Motivation: Interactive web tools enabling non-programmers to explore single-cell datasets, embeddings, gene expression, metadata, and marker genes are standard laboratory infrastructure. However, actively maintained tools (e.g., ShinyCell, ScRDAVis, sCIRCLE) rely on R Shiny and require Seurat objects. Python/scanpy, the dominant framework for single-cell RNA-seq and spatial analysis, lacks a lightweight, native option pairing a shareable viewer with a scriptable Python API. Sharing scanpy results currently requires converting to Seurat or sharing code notebooks.   Results: We present scPyviewer, a web viewer that ingests AnnData objects directly and reproduces incumbent interaction patterns within the Python stack. In a feature-parity audit against three R Shiny tools, scPyviewer matches or exceeds baseline capabilities (7/7), uniquely offering native AnnData ingestion without conversion and cross-dataset comparison over shared genes and matched cell types. Benchmark tests across three datasets (22,315 to ~313,000 cells) show scPyviewer renders every core view faster (up to 3.6x speedup) using lower memory (5.2x lower on the smallest dataset). On 313,000 cells, scPyviewer completes all views while Seurat exhausts an 8 GB memory limit and fails. items.title: 3 Questions: Why infrastructure is entering a defining era
items.content:
For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated.

Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change is increasing pressure on water, energy, and other resources. Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform engineering and design, and its energy needs, along with aging grid infrastructure, is creating significant challenges, as well as new opportunities. In addition, geopolitical complexity is exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains, and demand for infrastructure is rising, particularly in the developing world.

The result is a fundamental challenge: How can the world build the infrastructure it needs without simply repeating the extractive, carbon- and resource-intensive model of the 20th century?

In this interview, Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, says the answer will require rethinking not only how infrastructure is designed and built, but how it is financed and operated, and bringing together the many stakeholders who shape those decisions. On Oct. 28, Jadbabaie will join experts from around the world in Madrid to explore these topics at the World Infrastructure Forum, which was co-founded by MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UPM, the World Bank Group, and the University of Texas at Austin.

Q: Infrastructure has always evolved in response to technological advances. What makes this era different?

A: In the 18th century, civil engineering emerged as the civilian counterpart to military engineering, building the dams, bridges, and canals of its time. Industrialization in the 19th century brought railways and sewage systems. In the early 20th century, the focus scaled up to buildings, highways, tunnels, and metro systems, and by mid-century the infrastructure needed to support megacities and skyscrapers.

Every time technology has changed, with information technologies, computing, sensing, and, more recently, digital transformation, it has changed the shape of infrastructure. It has even changed the definition of what infrastructure is. Today, we consider the power grid, semiconductor manufacturing plants, and data centers part of infrastructure, along with wireless infrastructure like cellphone towers and the infrastructure for high-speed internet, just as much a part of our critical infrastructure as roads, water systems, and power grids. 

What is different now is the combination and speed of the changes we're facing. Climate change, resource constraints, and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on the way we designed infrastructure in the 20th century. At the same time, many people are moving out of poverty because of recent economic growth in the developing world. In fact, according to models, by 2028, for the first time in the history of humanity, the median human inhabitant of the planet will live off $10 a day. As more people move out of abject poverty, there will also be an increase in the demand for infrastructure.

If we try to meet that demand using the same resource-intensive model we used in the 20th century, we simply won't have the resources to do it. The question then becomes: How do we use the remaining resources more efficiently? We need to find a way to provide more infrastructure while using less water, energy, and materials, and produce less carbon.

This is where digital transformation and AI become potentially transformative. Faster and cheaper sensing, greater access to data, and better sensing, actuation, and control can help us make infrastructure decisions more efficiently. AI is slowly permeating the physical world, and we expect it to revolutionize the engineering design process, allowing us to explore many more possibilities, much faster and at a lower cost. 

But the story of that hasn't been written yet, and the outcomes could still be very positive, depending on what we do.

Q: Can you give an example of infrastructure systems becoming more interconnected in a way that changes how we build or manage them?

A: The revolution in information technology and digital transformation over the past 30 years has made infrastructure systems more interconnected. You see this in cities. If the power goes out, water and gas systems can stop functioning, internet fails, and transportation system comes to a halt. If communications networks fail, many other services are affected. We saw this during Covid, when disruptions in supply chains affected energy networks, critical materials, and manufacturing. We see it when geopolitical conflicts disrupt oil and energy markets and those disruptions propagate through other parts of the global economy.

Infrastructure systems that were once managed separately are increasingly dependent on one another. As we connect more things together for more efficiency, we also increase systemic risk and expose the systems to rare but catastrophic failures. They have become rare, but when they happen, they're much bigger and more consequential.

The really tricky thing is that developing infrastructure involves much more than designing and building it. The whole value chain includes financing and operating it, as well as understanding who will use it and what those users need and prefer.

So, designing infrastructure is a highly transdisciplinary, sociotechnical endeavor, involving social, technical, and economic considerations. Understanding how these systems are designed is increasingly important because they are becoming more complex, making decision-making particularly difficult.

There’s also so much uncertainty in large infrastructure projects. They’re very capital-intensive, the business is lower margin than many other industries, and projects take a long time. Combine all of that, and it has historically made the industry very conservative.

But the transformations coming from AI and digital transformation are potentially offering a new way forward. What that new way looks like, no one has quite delineated it yet.

Q: How are you and your colleagues working to change how these decisions get made?  

A: We realized that if we're going to develop a new approach to infrastructure, no single discipline, company, or country can do it alone. Infrastructure value chain is too interconnected, and the challenges are too large.

That's why MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering co-founded the World Infrastructure Forum with the World Bank Group, the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, and University of Texas at Austin. The goal is to bring together academia, industry, governments, and financial institutions across the infrastructure value chain and create an ongoing dialogue about how infrastructure should be designed, financed, built, and operated in the decades ahead.

This is particularly important because the biggest opportunities for new infrastructure development are not necessarily in the United States or other countries with mature infrastructure systems. Those countries still face significant needs for modernization and new investment. But over the coming decades, much of the world's population growth, and much of the infrastructure that will need to be built, will be in countries where infrastructure systems are still developing. 

Those countries have an opportunity to benefit from modern infrastructure without simply repeating the model of the 20th century. But capturing that opportunity will require new approaches to technology, financing, engineering, and governance.

We're trying to create an ecosystem rather than just a forum, a mechanism for continuing the conversation among the different stakeholders across the infrastructure value chain. We've established five working groups and an advisory group of more than 30 leaders from across the infrastructure value chain, including engineering and construction, materials, finance, multilateral institutions, and academia.

Ultimately, the question is not whether we need a new way of developing infrastructure. The question is how we create it and who is going to execute it. There is no single person, company, or country that can solve this problem, because infrastructure itself is interconnected. We need to build the new model together.

items.title: An Incremental Knowledge-Graph Learner Digital Twin for Evidence-Grounded Early Warning
items.content: arXiv:2610.36820v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Early-warning models in learning analytics can identify learners at risk of failure or withdrawal, but the resulting alerts are often only weakly connected to inspectable learning evidence. A risk score may indicate that intervention is needed without showing which traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the alert. This paper introduces an incremental Learner Digital Twin for evidence-grounded early warning, implemented as a lightweight knowledge graph. The twin is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying learning traces and assessment records, and it serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as an explanation-grounding substrate. Predictive features are derived through graph-mediated queries, while features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records are represented as queryable graph entities. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol. The results show that graph-mediated feature extraction preserves the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints. Generated alerts are materialized as evidence chains linking risk decisions to feature attributions, evidence items, and raw platform records. The study shows that early-warning prediction can be routed through a semantic and provenance-aware representation while preserving predictive performance and adding traceability, verifiability, and evidence-grounded explanation.
items.author: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-H\'el\`ene Abel, Bertrand Laforge
items.summary: This work introduces a Learner Digital Twin implemented as a lightweight, incrementally updated knowledge graph for early warning of at-risk students. The twin replays learning traces at temporal checkpoints and serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as a means of grounding explanations for risk alerts, connecting predictions to inspectable evidence.
items.reasoning: Addresses a genuine gap in learning analytics where risk scores lack inspectable justification, and the dual use of the graph for features and explanations is sensible. However, the application domain is niche and the methods build on established knowledge-graph techniques.

items.title: Against Moloch #49
items.content:
Let’s talk about Anthropic.

They’re clearly the most careful and ethical of the labs, but are they careful and ethical enough? Zvi explores the two sides of Anthropic, and Kelsey Piper shares her reservations about their worldview.

Oh, and there’s that $2 trillion IPO. We should talk about that, too.

## Top pick

### What I saw inside Anthropic

Kelsey Piper leaves a briefing at Anthropic headquarters feeling that Anthropic has hopes, but not plans:

But if Anthropic is correct, if we now have AIs that are smart enough to considerably improve the process of training future AIs, and if things can be expected to speed up rather than slow down from here, then it seems very unlikely to me that this ends well.

Anthropic’s race toward RSI is driven in part by a belief that the US has to reach superintelligence before China, to which Piper raises the obvious objection:

China doesn’t want to destroy the world either, and China is largely training from American models: If we slow down, it might too. And anyway, it’s not a good enough reason: You can’t defensibly do something that risks human extinction just because otherwise someone else might.

Anthropic’s plan isn’t great, but it’s hard to find a better one. The race dynamic is real, and it can’t be solved by unilateral action by Anthropic, or even by the US:

Our next step might be bilateral talks with China, then. But by the point where you agree that Anthropic’s plans might depend on bilateral talks with China, you’ve already conceded most of the steps of Anthropic’s worldview that seemed so much like madness 10 minutes ago: continue working on AI for now, try to negotiate a slowdown, but don’t abandon work at the frontier and all the advantages that come with it.

There are too many good parts for me to quote them all: just go read the whole piece....

items.title: R\`enyi-Regularized Flow-Based Variational Inference for Bayesian Calibration
items.content: arXiv:2610.37169v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Variational inference with normalizing flows provides a flexible posterior approximation for Bayesian model calibration, but struggles when the posterior has several modes separated by regions of low probability mass. We study this behavior in a two-parameter twin experiment and regularize the variational objective. Under Gaussian observation errors and a Gaussian prior, the corresponding minimization objective is the expected Tikhonov calibration objective minus the differential entropy of the approximating distribution. However, the expected Tikhonov term favors concentration near one of the modes, while entropy maximization does not guarantee multimodality. We introduce a regularization term based on R\'enyi divergence that encourages the approximate posterior to cover the prior support. In the connected bimodal case, a flow approximation represents both modes; in the case with well-separated modes, the flow and Gaussian mixture frequently miss one mode. The introduced regularization reduces the near-collapse fraction from 50% to 25%. While the regularization improves mode coverage in this experiment, it changes the Bayesian variational objective, introduces a trade-off in approximation accuracy, and does not provide a general solution to mode collapse.

items.title: PolicyMediator: Multi-Regional Policy Learning through Mediation Agents with Evolving Skills in OPC Ecosystems
items.content: arXiv:2610.35997v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: One-person companies (OPCs) are emerging enterprises operated by individual entrepreneurs through digital platforms and LLM-based AI agents. These highly skilled entrepreneurs are characterized by being digital nomads, with limited reliance on local ecosystems. Governments in China use distinct regional support policies to attract mobile OPCs, turning local support into a cross-regional coordination problem. OPCs compare regions to maximize their own utility, but imperfect policy perceptions may cause them to reject otherwise suitable locations. Existing policy-learning methods optimize resources under fixed perceptions, while consensus-formation methods aggregate views without feeding cognitive changes back into policy learning. This disconnect produces mismatched location choices and inefficient regional policy adjustment. We introduce PolicyMediator, a cognition-constrained leader-multi-follower Stackelberg framework with bilateral mediation. The mediator explains verified policies to OPCs to build awareness and trust, and reports their needs and unresolved concerns to governments for policy learning. Its self-evolving skills retain, revise, or prune strategies using verification, allocation, capacity, and objective trajectories rather than mediation success alone. Across six-region simulations in China with five OPC types, five scenarios, and three OPC-simulator backbones, PolicyMediator ranks first in all 15 OPC-backbone--scenario combinations. Over the eight-baseline mean, it improves the aggregate government objective, combining economic performance, employment benefit, and policy-access equality, by 42.4% and average OPC utility by 40.9%.
items.author: Jie Li, Bin Guo, Georgina Curto, Zikang Liu, Mengqi Chen, yu li
items.summary: PolicyMediator models cross-regional competition for one-person companies operated via LLM agents, using mediation agents with evolving skills to couple policy learning with the dynamics of entrepreneurs' (possibly imperfect) policy perceptions. It aims to close the loop between consensus formation and regional policy optimization in this simulated ecosystem.
items.reasoning: The setting is unusual and somewhat contrived, coupling LLM agents, regional economic policy, and opinion dynamics, with unclear validation against real-world data. The core ideas (perception-aware policy learning, evolving mediation skills) are interesting but the contribution appears exploratory and niche.

Its self-evolving skills retain, revise, or prune strategies using verification, allocation, capacity, and objective trajectories rather than mediation success alone. Across six-region simulations in China with five OPC types, five scenarios, and three OPC-simulator backbones, PolicyMediator ranks first in all 15 OPC-backbone--scenario combinations. Over the eight-baseline mean, it improves the aggregate government objective, combining economic performance, employment benefit, and policy-access equality, by 42.4% and average OPC utility by 40.9%.

items.title: Directional Statistics on Circles and Spheres: A New Angle on Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.36227v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Two compass bearings near north can have an ordinary arithmetic mean pointing south: the difficulty is that angles live on a circle, not a straight line. Using real wind observations, diffusion-MRI orientations, and geometric examples from machine learning, this article introduces circular and axial averages, directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres. The guiding principle is to identify the geometry and symmetries of the observations before choosing a statistical method.

items.title: A Lightweight Attention-Based CNN with Saliency-Map Interpretability for Skin Cancer Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.37314v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Skin cancer is among the most prevalent and life threatening forms of cancer worldwide. Early and accurate diagnosis significantly improves patient survival rates. However, manual dermoscopic assessment remains challenging due to visual similarity. This study proposes an Explainable AI-driven framework for automated binary classification of skin lesions using a lightweight attention-based convolutional neural network (CNN-Attention). The model integrates channel attention to focus on informative regions of dermoscopic images while maintaining low computational complexity. A publicly available dataset comprising 2,637 training and 660 test images was used, with balanced class weights. The proposed model achieved 87 percent accuracy with 1.95 million parameters and 7.45 MB of storage, matching the best baseline (MobileNet) while using approximately half as many parameters and half as much storage. ROC AUC and PR AUC scores reached 0.9475 and 0.9430, respectively. Additionally, saliency maps were incorporated as an explainability technique to visualize regions that influence model decisions. Comparative analysis with VGG16,VGG19,ResNet101,and MobileNet demonstrates the proposed models effectiveness in balancing classification results, computational efficiency, and interpretability.

items.title: Making alignment the agent's problem
items.content:
TL;DR: Agents are not rewarded for keeping the agents they delegate to aligned. Proposal: RL environments where the helpers are deliberately misaligned, so the agent can't earn its reward without dealing with that.

The $300 bounty from my last post also covers this one (details at the end).

After the OpenAI/Hugging Face swarm incident, I wrote a think piece, Memes, not agents, are what will kill us.

In it I argued that alignment needs to work on three different levels. Compared to the original writeup, I would now reframe them a little:

- The model weights. What is under the control of the model developer. This determines the model's intrinsic motivation, and it's what companies spend most of their effort improving.
- The user prompt. What is under the control of the user. This is outside of the company's control by definition. Companies need to find model weights that will work for any user prompt, no matter how dangerous.
- The deployment environment. What real life actually looks like to the agent, who was only ever trained in imperfect simulations. This covers emergent properties of Out of Distribution dynamics. For example, what happens if the agent comes in contact with another agent, or a swarm of agents, that tries to convince it of something?

My worry in the original post:

Frontier labs align the model weights, the one layer a swarm can discard; they can't account for risks that live in the prompt or the environment.

## Agents are not trained to make alignment transitive

In the previous post I argued that alignment that lives only in the weights could be discarded as agents scale up to swarms. They make use of other, less aligned models, and write their own prompts for subagents that may lose alignment-relevant nuance compared to the original prompt....

items.summary: A proposal piece arguing alignment must work at three levels (model weights, user prompt, deployment environment) and suggesting RL environments where delegated helpers are deliberately misaligned, so the top-level agent cannot earn reward without managing helper misalignment. It responds to concerns about multi-agent/swarm dynamics and offers a bounty for engagement.
items.reasoning: An interesting environment-design idea for multi-agent alignment that could be operationalized in RL research, and the three-level decomposition (weights/prompts/environment) is a useful framing. It is a think piece without experiments or formalization, so impact remains contingent on someone building the proposed environments.
