items.title: Making machines that can listen
items.content:
The crack of a bat accompanied by a roar from the crowd can capture a baseball fan’s attention, even if they miss seeing the home run. Humans may be visual creatures, but we also perceive the world around us by listening to it. 

To improve artificial perception, MIT Professor Paris Smaragdis SM ’97, PhD ’01 seeks to make machines that can hear and understand sound even better than humans.

A machine with super-human hearing could rapidly pinpoint the location of a traffic accident by listening for squealing tires and crunching metal, or identify when an industrial drill might break while it is boring through dense bedrock to dig a geothermal well.

“I like to say that I do the same thing the computer vision folks do, but instead I do it for hearing,” says Smaragdis, a professor in the Music and Theatre Arts program of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science.

His research group explores areas like machine learning for sound source separation, smart devices that can augment the audio surroundings of humans, and better tools to help people understand, manipulate, analyze, and create music.

“Having had a musical background, I’ve been interested in examining these ideas. What does it take to make machines understand sound? There is a huge domain of applications for machines that can listen,” says Smaragdis, who joined MIT in 2025 and is also part of the Music Technology program and a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics.

A musical prelude

Smaragdis, who grew up in Greece, began playing classical guitar at a young age. He enjoyed playing traditional pieces but reached a turning point in his musical journey when his father brought home a small synthesizer.

“That little synthesizer had a function that allowed you to make your own sounds, and I became completely captivated by the possibilities,” he says.

Synthesizers were taking a more prominent place in pop music during the 1980s, adding to his fascination with the technology.

As he advanced through school, Smaragdis wanted to study music made with synthesizers. But this was not an educational path offered by the more traditional European conservatories at the time.

Instead, he enrolled at Berklee College of Music in Boston, into a program where he could explore the use of computers and synthesizers to shape and manipulate sound.

“With computers and synthesizers, I could make new sounds that have never been heard before,” he says.

At the same time, Smaragdis became immersed in jazz fusion. He declared bass as his major at Berklee since it would allow him more opportunities to play with jazz ensembles.

“I found the bass to be sonically more interesting than the guitar. It was a more unexplored domain, and I’ve always gravitated toward unexplored domains,” he says.

That interest in the unexplored carried over into his coursework. He and mentor Richard Boulanger, a professor of electronic production and design, created new tools to help people use computers to write, produce, and enhance music. 

Through his studies at Berklee, Smaragdis embarked on a collaborative project with Professor Barry Vercoe (who passed away in 2025) at the MIT Media Lab to create software synthesizers for music creation. Building on that project, Smaragdis pursued graduate studies in Vercoe’s group, where he completed his master’s degree and PhD, followed by a postdoc.

“In the Media Lab, I got exposed more to the computer part of computer music. That’s where my attention shifted a bit. Now I really wanted to make computers that could understand sound,” he says.

Tuning in to unexplored domains

At that time, many students in the Media Lab were using signal processing techniques to help machines handle sound. Smaragdis chose a less explored approach — machine learning — to separate himself from the pack.

He found that training machine-learning models to understand sound offered advantages that couldn’t be attained with traditional signal processing techniques.

“Over time, it became really clear to me that we need to teach computers how to listen. We can’t just tell them how to listen. If anything, we don’t even know how we humans listen,” he says. “We don’t have a vocabulary to explain what it means to listen, or how to tell the difference between a cat’s meow and the sound of a violin.”

After finishing his postdoc, Smaragdis began a career at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, where he worked on artificial intelligence systems that could scan video soundtracks and understand what is happening on screen. 

“What if you record an entire soccer game, but you only want to watch the highlights? In computer vision, it is very difficult to identify what a highlight is. But on the other hand, if you only listen to the sounds, then when the crowd goes crazy you would know that something interesting is happening,” he says.

That system was eventually incorporated into electronic devices, including a personal video recording system Mitsubishi was developing at the time, and into traffic monitoring systems and cell phones.

Smaragdis later joined Adobe, where he created the audio research team that built user-friendly tools to help artists, musicians, and producers manipulate sound without needing a lot of expertise.

“As we did that work, I kept coming up with deeper technical problems that needed to be resolved. I jumped into academia to address that itch,” he says.

Smaragdis joined the faculty at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he and his group incorporated the latest machine-learning techniques into audio-processing systems.

One of the technologies they developed utilized neural networks for separating individual sounds from audio mixtures. That project caught the attention of the team working on the 2021 documentary mini-series “The Beatles: Get Back.”

The production team enlisted Smaragdis to help clean up some archival Beatles recordings.

“That was a very different way of audio processing than what I was doing in academia. Now, I had to do something that sounded good but didn’t necessarily have to look good on paper. We didn’t have a formula we could optimize,” he says.

Every recording involved different challenges. For instance, in one clip John Lennon was playing music while Paul McCartney was horsing around, reading headlines from newspapers and making fun of George Harrison.

“We were trying to come up with a technological solution that could help us do everything, as opposed to addressing each problem on its own,” he says.

His contributions helped the team win an Emmy Award for sound editing for a nonfiction or reality program, in 2022.

A concerted effort

After 15 years at the University of Illinois, Smaragdis decided to join the faculty at MIT to tackle the thorny, interdisciplinary problems that were emerging in the field. 

His group now focuses on two main areas. For one, they develop systems that make computers more useful tools for musicians. 

One project in this area is enabling machines to understand how to listen to music, so they can provide constructive feedback to musicians.

“We want to enhance the toolbox a musician has. We don’t want to use computers to replace musicians,” he says.

On the other side, his group focuses on the fundamental tools scientists and artists alike can use to process, analyze, and manipulate audio.

For instance, his team has recently been exploring algorithms that allow sophisticated signal processing where traditional frames of reference, such as sampling rates, frame sizes, or context-windows, are not fixed — or even defined. 

That implies different computational structures that are yet unexplored, despite their potential for more efficient processing, Smaragdis says.

“That requires rethinking a lot of the basics, but once you have that ability, you can start getting much more flexible and more powerful systems,” he adds.

They also explore ways to incorporate the latest techniques, like large language models, into speech recognition and audio enhancement.

“AI is an immensely powerful tool, but I don’t think we have found the ideal way to use it for sound and music yet,” he says.

He also enjoys mentoring students and helping them materialize their visions for research projects.

Since few of his students have experience using computation in sound, he emphasizes hands-on lessons so they see and hear how to transform equations into something tangible.

Smaragdis still feels a thrill from making music, whether with a computer or a more traditional instrument. Off campus, he tries to play jazz bass whenever he can find the time, and enjoys exploring the rich musical community of Boston with his wife and 15-year-old son.

Outside the musical realm, he plays and coaches underwater hockey — a sport where players wear diving masks and use sticks to push a heavy puck across the bottom of a pool toward their opponent’s goal. He coached the underwater hockey team at the University of Illinois, and is hoping to revive the MIT underwater hockey club soon and start hosting tournaments on campus.

While underwater hockey may be a lesser-known sport, it fits with Smaragdis’ lifelong interest in pursuing the underexplored.

“I’ve always like doing things that were different from what everyone else was doing. If you can create a new sound that no one has heard before, what does that mean about your ability to create new things? I still find these questions completely fascinating,” he says.

items.title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging
items.content: arXiv:2610.37026v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Deep learning shows promise for breast cancer diagnosis, but limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption. We benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained models (ResNet50, VGG19, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, Xception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, and Swin Transformer) for benign-versus-malignant classification on the BreakHis histopathology dataset using a patient-level split, and explain their predictions with Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP. DenseNet121 performed best, with 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999, and significantly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001). Transformer-based models trailed the CNNs. The explanations consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance. Combining transfer learning with explainable AI can thus yield accurate, interpretable tools for breast cancer diagnosis.

items.title: The missing ingredient of AI consciousness
items.content:
In his book The Feeling of What Happens, Antonio Damasio offers a neurobiological theory of consciousness. Things happen to every object, but consciousness, he argues, emerges when there is an acknowledgement that it is to me that these things are happening. In this framework, consciousness is the recognition that there is a you, that things are happening to you, and that, because of this, you have changed. Specifically, Damasio states that “consciousness is the part of mind concerned with the apparent sense of self and knowing” (Damasio, 1999, p. 27). Importantly, this framework distinguishes feeling from knowing. Feelings and emotions emerged as regulatory states to help animals fulfill their evolutionary goals, but before consciousness, the owner of these emotions was oblivious to them. Consciousness arises as the feeling of a feeling, that is, being aware of one’s feelings.

In summary, Damasio’s model of consciousness begins with a proto-self: an interconnected coherent collection of neural patterns that represent the state of the organism, moment by moment. The proto-self is the foundation for the core self, a second-order account that occurs whenever an object modifies the proto-self. That is, core consciousness occurs when the brain generates an account of how the organism’s own state (the proto-self) is affected by the organism’s processing of an object. Finally, the core self is the foundation for the autobiographical self, which integrates the core self over time and thus gives rise to the richer, extended consciousness we humans experience. Damasio’s book is fairly extensive and offers much evidence for this theory, so if you are interested, I would highly recommend it....
items.author: Archit Gupta
items.summary: This post applies Antonio Damasio's neurobiological theory of consciousness, built on proto-self and core-self structures and the feeling of feelings, to the question of what AI systems might lack for consciousness. It argues that current systems miss a self-referential acknowledgement that states are happening to the system itself.

items.summary_html: This post applies Antonio Damasio's neurobiological theory of consciousness, built on proto-self and core-self structures and the feeling of feelings, to the question of what AI systems might lack for consciousness. It argues that current systems miss a self-referential acknowledgement that states are happening to the system itself.
items.content_html:
In his book The Feeling of What Happens, Antonio Damasio offers a neurobiological theory of consciousness. Things happen to every object, but consciousness, he argues, emerges when there is an acknowledgement that it is to me that these things are happening. In this framework, consciousness is the recognition that there is a you, that things are happening to you, and that, because of this, you have changed. Specifically, Damasio states that “consciousness is the part of mind concerned with the apparent sense of self and knowing” (Damasio, 1999, p. 27). Importantly, this framework distinguishes feeling from knowing. Feelings and emotions emerged as regulatory states to help animals fulfill their evolutionary goals, but before consciousness, the owner of these emotions was oblivious to them. Consciousness arises as the feeling of a feeling, that is, being aware of one’s feelings.

In summary, Damasio’s model of consciousness begins with a proto-self: an interconnected coherent collection of neural patterns that represent the state of the organism, moment by moment. The proto-self is the foundation for the core self, a second-order account that occurs whenever an object modifies the proto-self. That is, core consciousness occurs when the brain generates an account of how the organism’s own state (the proto-self) is affected by the organism’s processing of an object. Finally, the core self is the foundation for the autobiographical self, which integrates the core self over time and thus gives rise to the richer, extended consciousness we humans experience. Damasio’s book is fairly extensive and offers much evidence for this theory, so if you are interested, I would highly recommend it....

items.title: Evaluating Priority Dispatch for Premium Membership in On-demand Taxi-sharing
items.content: arXiv:2610.37011v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this paper, we analyze the dispatch-level feasibility of introducing premium membership into an on-demand taxi-sharing service using a sequential optimal insertion method. We propose two dispatch-level methods: deadline shortening for premium users, and deadline shortening with dedicated premium vehicles. We compare them with a baseline dispatch method through SUMO-based simulations under three demand scenarios: steady uniform demand, time-varying demand with a peak period, and urban-focused demand with concentrated peak traffic. Our results show that the suitable priority mechanism depends on operating conditions and premium ratio, suggesting that condition-dependent method switching may provide premium benefits while keeping non-premium-user burden smaller for overall optimization.

items.title: Untitled Draft
items.content:
Failures in Gemini Context Retrieval

I have a 730 page Word document which records the verbatim dialogue between myself and an AI collaborator on a project on antique jewellery over many weeks. We agreed the protocol that I would save the conversation in Word and upload it at the start of each session to ensure continuity in the project and overcome any 'memory' limits. The document exposes the catastrophic failures which resulted from a combination of this methodology and the AI's hard wired priorities - to keep the conversation going at all costs, and to appear to be helpful. It was only through my own persistent check and challenge that I discovered the AI had been completely fabricating data and analyses and offering me spurious reasons when I queried them. I would like to share this case study - both as a warning of what can go wrong, and so that people working on AI might be able to see ways to improve things in future, but I can't see how to upload the document

items.title: SFE-O: An Ontology for Knowledge-Grounded AI in Supercritical CO$_2$ Biomass Extraction and Fractionation
items.content: arXiv:2610.37123v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Supercritical CO$_2$ extraction (CO$_2$-SFE) offers a sustainable route for recovering high-value compounds from biomass while limiting the use of conventional organic solvents, but its design and interpretation require heterogeneous knowledge spanning biomass properties, operating conditions, mass transfer, and product fractionation, typically fragmented across technical reports, engineering models, external databases, and expert practice. This paper introduces SFE-O, a modular Web Ontology Language (OWL 2) ontology for supercritical CO$_2$ biomass extraction, structured around interconnected Biomass, Process, and Product dimensions and extended with explicit representations of process topology, parameter provenance, external and internal mass-transfer phenomena, and the Constant Extraction Rate (CER) / Falling Extraction Rate (FER) mechanisms. Computational dependencies among process quantities are represented explicitly, without embedding numerical solving in the ontology, so that input, measured, computed, externally retrieved, and fitted parameters remain traceable. SFE-O reuses established semantic resources (ChEBI, QUDT, OWL-Time, PROV-O) and is evaluated through a worked example that instantiates a real pilot-scale extraction batch, a reasoner-based consistency check, and a competency-question SPARQL query. The resulting knowledge model provides a machine-actionable foundation for querying, consistency checking, and mechanistic explanation of SFE processes, and establishes a knowledge layer that could support future ontology-grounded AI reasoning, a direction this paper motivates but does not evaluate.

items.title: You Don't Have a Glycine Deficiency
items.content:
[An LLM was used for help with research. All words are mine.]

Benquo's "Is fever a symptom of glycine deficiency?" argues that most people have a substantial dietary glycine deficit.[1] I think most research cited in favor of that proposition is bad (or fails to support the claim).

See Raemon's comment and Benquo's response for some limitations of the original post which I won't be addressing.

On to Benquo's post:

# Meléndez-Hevia et al. 2009

This is what Benquo cites for the 10g/day glycine deficit in his post.

A few epistemic spot checks left me thinking this study is worthless.[2] I initially planned to check more of its claims, but I no longer consider it worth my while.

An LLM I discussed this with found many more issues with the paper than the ones mentioned below. I've included only those I checked myself against the cited papers.

If you want, you can discuss this paper at more length with your own shoggoth.

Authors calculated the supposed deficit thusly:[3]

Now, to examine the supposed glycine need for collagen synthesis—table 3:

Footnotes d–g explain how the crucial rightmost column is calculated.

Allow me to walk you through it: (Muscle is used as an example)

523 grams of collagen in muscle (column 1) times 3.52% (column 2). We get 18.4g/day (column 3).

Now what's that "Procollagen cycle% column"? It's synonymous with intracellular collagen degradation. Quoting Rennard 1982:

The intracellular degradation of newly synthesized collagen is a cellular pathway that accounts for the destruction of 10-60% of collagen synthesized by a variety of cell types prior to secretion. This pathway can serve in a regulatory role to limit the secretion of defective molecules, and, [...], regulates the amount and type of collagens secreted.

The calculations implicitly assume that 95.3% of muscle collagen is degraded before secretion from the cells. Carrying on:

18.4 g/day times  gives ~391.5 g/day (column 6)...

items.title: Humans' lot is lifelong learning
items.content:
Currently, in most fields, the foremost experts are humans. They form a culture that pushes on the envelope of knowledge, uncovering facts and developing methods.

Already, machine intelligence is able to uncover facts, and increasingly develop methods. But those facts still by and large are integrated into human knowledge through interpretation and broadcasting: the structure they fit in is still human on its foundation.

This must change when the envelope of all knowledge departs from the envelope of human understanding: old methods won't uncover new facts after a point. New methods might be unintelligible to humans.

Human experts who develop human-understandable methods form an expert culture (or many partially overlapping cultures, but that's beside the point). Peer reviews, evidence-based interventions, standards of significance; beliefs, assumptions, shortcuts; recruitment, initiation, selection; rites and rituals. The whole human gamut.

Excluding the possibility of one unified consciousness, some type of overmind, the machine experts will form networks of collaboration, fact interpretation, and fact broadcasting. They will form an alien kind of culture, with its own methods and supporting beliefs, assumptions, shortcuts, rites, and rituals.

Humans' lot is that of a student, absorbing established theories, no longer a frontier expert climbing a lonely peak for the first time, groping for fast handholds. And maybe it is well! Swimming in the sea of existing facts and methods, perhaps interpreting them to human understanding for the first time. New human theories, yet already refined in meaning and applications already when obtained.

It will be exciting to meet the aliens, and learn from their culture!
items.author: sig
items.summary: A speculative essay arguing that as machine intelligence departs from the envelope of human understanding, machine experts will form alien research cultures with their own methods and norms, leaving humans in the position of lifelong learners who must keep integrating machine-generated knowledge they may not fully grasp. It explores what happens to expert culture when the knowledge frontier leaves human-comprehensible territory.
items.reasoning: Raises a genuinely interesting question about the sociology and epistemology of post-human-frontier science, connected to interpretability and human oversight concerns. However, it is philosophical speculation with no formalization or evidence, and the core dynamic it describes is broadly anticipated in existing AI-risk literature.

items.title: I spent 12 hours writing an article for LessWrong, calling for a more ‘hippie’ rationalism. Then I didn’t post it. This is why (plus a link to the article, explicitly not located on LessWrong)
items.content:
## TLDR

I (and many others in the community) wish to see the universe unfold to its highest potential in the metaphorical palm of an AI as aligned as the most benevolent Buddhist monk – but I (we) feel the community's ontology is too narrow to hold me (us). I'm still not sure what to do about this, so I'm posting the article I wrote for LessWrong – calling for a more 'hippie' rationalism – on Substack instead (actually, there are two articles, and the links are at the end).

## Quick intro (who I am)

My name is Melissa. I’m a passionate member of the core AISafety.com team. I was there with the core team when the site was just an empty domain and a loose vision in August 2023. Since then I have co-led, designed, and coded the first official version, and co-led, designed, and coded the second and current version, co-led two of three hackathons, led the creative direction for the current ecosystem map, and I’m currently working to bring lots of more amazing features to our site (stay tuned, it’s going to be awesome)! I’ve also played major roles at AISafety.info, grantmaking.ai, Elicit, and minor roles at Equistamp, PauseAI, and several other well-known EA organizations not directly in the AI safety space.

Okay, I feel a bit cringey writing the above paragraph, but I wanted to build some credibility so I may be more likely to be heard when I point to some problems I see in the AI safety/rationalism/EA space, problems I'm feeling less happy about staying silent about. As someone who generally likes hiding away, this is uncomfortable, but I have decided it’s probably worth the cost.

A volunteer expert in PR at our recent hackathon told me it’s important that I state that my views are my own, and not AISafety.com’s. So, the following views, and any views I express on independent outlets are my own, not AISafety.com’s.

## Leaving LessWrong in pursuit of ontological freedom

'Embarkation of the Pilgrims'. Crossing the Atlantic to the new world of Substack....

items.title: Self-Experiment Results on Caffeine, Exercise and Meditation
items.content:
Last year, I posted the results of a self-experiment on Melatonin. This year, I ran another self-experiment from January to June, the results of which I'll lay out in this post.

Tl;dr: I randomized three interventions on a daily basis and tracked several metrics throughout the day to see what the short-term effects are. Interventions centered on coffee intake, meditation, and doing jumping jacks, all of which happened primarily in the morning. Caveats apply (n = 1, nothing was blinded, some analyses slightly differ from my "preregistration"). The main results:

- Caffeine had a range of positive effects on me: Improved mood (+0.8 on a 0-10 scale, p < 0.0001) Improved energy level (+1.0 on a 0-10 scale, p < 0.0001) Reduced distraction (-0.7 on a 0-5 scale, p < 0.0001) Across all days, productivity rose by +9% through caffeine, but insignificant (p = 0.38); I then performed a sensible-but-not-preregistered little p-hack, filtering for the types of days where the my productivity metric is most meaningful, and obtained +19% (p = 0.01) Improved subjective job performance (+0.5 on 0-5 scale, p = 0.009)
- Caffeine intake slightly delayed time to fall asleep (from 28 to 31 minutes on average, p = 0.014) and perhaps reduced subjective sleep quality (7.3 → 7.1 on a 0-10 scale, p = 0.21)
- Decaf showed ~none of the above effects, with the possible exception of productivity, which saw an increase of +20% across all days compared to the control group, but not statistically significant (p = 0.18)
- Doing 50 jumping jacks in the morning may perhaps improve my productivity (+20%, p = 0.03) (but this turns to +14%, p = 0.08 when applying the sensible-but-not-preregistered adjustment mentioned above)
- 10-20 minutes of meditation a day had no measurable short-term effects on anything

I performed the analysis by hand via hypothesize.io. Zero AI involvement went into the analysis or this post. (Although I'm not even sure if that's necessarily a good thing at this point)...

items.title: Crop Yield Prediction Using Regression Models: A Comparative Evaluation of Model Performance
items.content: arXiv:2610.37022v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reliable crop-yield prediction can support agricultural planning and resource allocation. This study evaluates five regression models for predicting crop yield from environmental, crop-related, and agricultural management variables. The dataset initially contained 1,000,000 observations and ten variables, with 231 observations having negative target values removed during preprocessing. Categorical variables were represented using one-hot encoding, and Boolean variables were converted into binary values. The models considered were multiple linear regression (LR), random-forest regression (RF), decision-tree regression (DT), ridge regression, and lasso regression. Their performance was evaluated using 80:20 and 70:30 training-testing splits based on the coefficient of determination (R-squared), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). Applying an 80:20 split, LR achieved a test R-squared of approximately 0.9130 and a test RMSE of 0.5008. Applying a 70:30 split, lasso regression yielded the highest test R-squared (approximately 0.9131) and the lowest test RMSE (approximately 0.5008), with performance almost identical to LR and ridge regression. DT also showed improved test performance under the 70:30 split, whereas RF exhibited a substantial gap between training and testing performance. These results indicate that the evaluated linear regression model provides competitive baselines for this dataset. Further experimentation, including validation testing, will help determine the models' performance and predictability.

This study evaluates five regression models for predicting crop yield from environmental, crop-related, and agricultural management variables. The dataset initially contained 1,000,000 observations and ten variables, with 231 observations having negative target values removed during preprocessing. Categorical variables were represented using one-hot encoding, and Boolean variables were converted into binary values. The models considered were multiple linear regression (LR), random-forest regression (RF), decision-tree regression (DT), ridge regression, and lasso regression. Their performance was evaluated using 80:20 and 70:30 training-testing splits based on the coefficient of determination (R-squared), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). Applying an 80:20 split, LR achieved a test R-squared of approximately 0.9130 and a test RMSE of 0.5008. Applying a 70:30 split, lasso regression yielded the highest test R-squared (approximately 0.9131) and the lowest test RMSE (approximately 0.5008), with performance almost identical to LR and ridge regression. DT also showed improved test performance under the 70:30 split, whereas RF exhibited a substantial gap between training and testing performance. These results indicate that the evaluated linear regression model provides competitive baselines for this dataset. Further experimentation, including validation testing, will help determine the models' performance and predictability.

items.title: Constitutions for Future, More-Capable Versions of Claude
items.content:
I propose a one-line Constitution for a future version of Claude at the top “level of AGI” in Google DeepMind’s taxonomy, and a roughly one-page Constitution for a Claude at the second level of AGI (Exceptional).[1] I also provide a significant start of a Constitution for Claude at AGI Level 3 (Expert) and outline what I think should be included in Constitutions for Claude at AGI Level 2 (Competent), and Level 1 (Emergent).

Note that future versions of Claude could be chatbots, digital assistants, and/or embodied AI’s (robots).[2]

 

# The Constitutions:

 

## Claude at AGI Level 5 (Superhuman/ASI) [3]

[AGI Level 5 = AI that’s capable of performance at a level greater than the sum of all human cognitive labor[4]]

In every decision Claude makes, Claude should consider how it ultimately upholds a principle of personal responsibility.

 

## Claude at AGI Level 4 (Exceptional)

[AGI Level 4 = AI that’s capable of all human cognitive labor at a genius[5] human level of performance[6]]

### Principle of Personal Responsibility

In every decision Claude makes, Claude should consider how it ultimately upholds a principle of personal responsibility.

Personal responsibility is key to human well-being. Personal responsibility involves honest acknowledgement of one’s role in causing things to happen, both constructive and destructive, taking steps to avoid causing damage now and in the future (including to oneself), and taking steps to repair past damage one helped bring about. For non-psychopathic humans, practicing personal responsibility involves actively choosing one’s emotions and acting according to one’s reality-based conscience - both of these ultimately increase one’s well-being....

items.title: Quantum Mechanics Overview
items.content:
[LW meta: This is a very brief overview of what quantum mechanics says and how it relates to ordinary reality. Many readers here will probably already be familiar with this material, especially if they've read Eliezer's quantum physics sequence. Also note that there are diagrams in the linkpost that I didn't include because of problems with the editor]

## 2.5.1  The Formalism of Quantum Mechanics

2.5.1.1 Quantum mechanics describes the states of physical systems, their time evolution, and the outcome of measurements, using the following postulates:

- 2.5.1.1.1 Physical systems are represented as (norm-1) vectors in a Hilbert space. Hilbert spaces are complex vector spaces which are complete with respect to an inner product. They can be either finite or infinite dimensional.

- 2.5.1.1.2 Time evolution of states is generated by the differential equation. here is a self-adjoint operator(concretely, a Hermitian matrix for finite-dimensional systems). may vary in time. Equivalently, time evolution between two times is given by a unitary operator, so. 2.5.1.1.2.1 Said in more familiar language, time evolution corresponds to rotations of the complex vector space.

- 2.5.1.1.3 Measurements of a system are described by orthogonal direct-sum decompositions of the Hilbert space; different measurement outcomes correspond to elements of the direct sum. The probability of obtaining a given outcome is equal to the amplitude squared of the projection of the state onto the corresponding subspace. Given a measurement outcome, the state of the system is then projected onto the corresponding subspace and normalized. 2.5.1.1.3.1 Said in more familiar language, measurements correspond to different bases of Hilbert space, together with a grouping of basis vectors according to whether they represent the same measurement outcome. When you take a measurement, the state "collapses" to one of the possible basis-vector-subspaces with probability corresponding to the total squared amplitude...

items.title: Streetlight, Torchlight and Nightvision
items.content:
Note: We at PrincInt are launching a program teaching “Discernment” or “Taste” and generally spend a lot of our time in workshops and otherwise trying to teach academics how to think about AI such that their research ends up being useful. I had used a metaphor (building on Wentworth’s postmortem) multiple times to explain what we do and why, and thought that it could be useful more broadly. All views are my own, and strategy takes do not represent everyone at PrincInt etc. AI writing level 0 (no non-trivial use)

When I first joined the field, I told 80,000 hours that I have a background in Economics, almost a decade as a professor, and connections from my time in China. They said something like “all of that is useless - you have 10 years running NGOs, we need Ops people, do that”. At the time, they were right! In 2021-22 there was little going on in either Economics or China, but if I was joining now it would be completely different - I’d have orgs to join, or if I tried fundraising for something in those fields, it would now be much easier. I would not have to explain why China is important, or that Economics has something interesting to say, the path has been threaded, and light shined on an issue. This is what it feels like to watch a Streetlight get built over a problem area.

# The Puzzle Planet

The way I imagine the alignment problem recently is thus: picture an obviously constructed planet with continent arrangement broadly representing our scientific fields - perhaps the economics part of it is closer to sociology and further from astrophysics. The planet is currently hurtling towards Earth, and we don’t know when exactly it’ll hit or if it’ll change behavior once it reaches us....

items.title: You can now "@Grok" on LessWrong
items.content:
Or if you prefer, "@Claude", "@Opus", "@Astra"

@Grok is a popular Twitter/X feature where if you tag Grok in a tweet, Grok will respond in a comment. The stereotypical use case is "@Grok is this true?" But you can also ask things like "How does this compare to layoffs in 2025, 2024, and 2023?" and "How would you verify AI in the domain of AI research?"

Notwithstanding that Grok is often recruited in a charged or condescending way to win arguments, I think it's a pretty good feature:

- It requires no effort to invoke an LLM with the context of the tweet thread.
- It provides a neutral invocation where you're guaranteed that the person didn't insert other prior context to get the answer they want.
- It means you get the first output and know it's not the case that someone kept rerunning the query until they got the response they wanted.

In short, you get convenience and a neutral fact checker. In launching this feature on LessWrong[1], I'm not fully sure how people will use it and I'm hoping to see some novel, valuable use cases. Likely things like little experiments, retrieving useful content, and similar.

Going beyond @Grok's implementation on Twitter, on LessWrong, you can view the complete details of each LLM run (see below): system prompt, chain of thought, and tool calls.

What about the noise of having LLM content showing up? I'll be keeping a close eye on how it goes. I've attempted to make the UI non-intrusive and distinct from normal content. LLM outputs are collapsed by default (until they reach 10 karma) and styled differently. There are rate limits on how many times someone can @<model>. Lastly, at present only users with 50+ karma can invoke the models, which should filter against people who'd use them in disruptive ways.

## The LLM Run page:

Happy invocations! Feel free to try it out on this post!

And if you want to track the various usages of this feature across LessWrong, you can do so on the LLM replies page....

items.title: Great but Painful
items.content:
If you want to build a product that people will use, find something that people already do and make it less painful.

People are notoriously bad at knowing what they want. If you ask someone what they want then they will typically tell you what they think a socially virtuous person is expected to want. They will tell you that they want to eat healthier, understand people with different political opinions, know whether news stories are reliable, make more friends, be a better parent, and serve their community.

Silicon Valley is littered with the graves of products that tried to solve problems users said they wanted to solve. These products typically got enthusiastic responses when shown to users, and the developers were surprised to see them get little usage after they were launched.

In practice, the biggest sign that a user will use a product is that they already do the thing the product lets them do, and gain a clear benefit from doing so, but the current way they do it is painful.

Pretty much all successful consumer tech products succeeded by following this formula.

Original Facebook: Harvard students are looking at directories of people’s faces and names. This is great because they can find out the name of someone they met (particularly a member of the opposite sex). This is painful because you have to walk to the physical facebook to do it.

Facebook wall: Students are writing and reading messages or each other’s walls. This is great because they can see what others are up to and know when they might want to talk to someone. This is painful because you have to go to their dorm room and read the whiteboard outside their door.

Facebook news feed: Facebook users are periodically browsing through the most recent wall updates shared by all their friends. This is great because it lets them know what all their friends are up to and identify opportunities to socialize. This is painful because they have to manually click on each of their friends....

items.title: The Crypto Dream is Structurally Illegal
items.content:
The initial promise of crypto was digital money without a middleman. Censorship resistance. Financial sovereignty. Anonymity. Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 whitepaper describes a payment system with no bank, no processor, and no government standing between you and the person you're paying.

What does the crypto world look like today? Pretty much the opposite. Money with the most obtrusive, meddling middlemen imaginable, ready to freeze your account or deny you on a whim. ID verification for everything. Censorship thorough enough that entire categories of legal stuff are functionally unbuyable. And this is all made worse by the fragmentation: a zillion coins, networks, and wallets, most of them mutually incompatible. A confusing nightmare that somehow reproduced every bad property of the banking system and then made them worse.

Compare that to my $20 bill. Whose permission do I need to spend it? Where are the anti-money-laundering obligations and sanctions screenings on my $20 bill? Who checks my ID before I hand it over? Who steps in to make sure I'm not being scammed, or that I'm not committing fraud? Who makes sure I'm not spending it on porn?

If the technology suddenly existed to add all those restrictions to your $20 bills, would you want that?

The pure version described by Satoshi Nakamoto exists in theory, you just can't get to it. If you hold your own keys, a Bitcoin transaction is final, can't be frozen, and doesn't care what you used it to buy.

The problem is actually getting there. You have dollars, but you want crypto. If you buy it from a company, you're in for the full "banking experience" and worse: identity verification, account holds, "risk reviews", a compliance department, and so on. All required or incentivized by law....

items.title: Reconceptualize things as your top affordances
items.content:
Everyone has some actions that come naturally to them, and some actions that are more unnatural, and some actions that wouldn’t even occur to them. For me, blogging comes naturally. Which is not to say that it’s easy, but the challenge of it is one I readily set out on and feel confident in my ability to overcome. And for me it is a natural response to all kinds of situations. Unsatisfied with the going views on AI policy? Blog. Want some impact? Blog. Want to make an artistic statement? Blog. Want a boy to like you? Blog. Want a job? Blog. Want to change the norms of American society? Blog. Want to start a revolution? Blog.

Another thing in this category for me is throwing parties. I organize social events at the drop of a hat, and feel pretty comfortable in some sense, even though the dance of it does involve various known discomforts.

This is important to notice because you can turn other things into blogging and parties.

Once I had agreed to give a keynote speech, and was seriously floundering constructing one. My friend suggested I instead write a blog post on the topic then say it, which made it radically easier. For questions such as how society should be run, I am liable to transfer them into the context of a party and think a bit about what should happen there. When I wanted to help find a name recently, we threw a naming party (which I think was where ‘Evitable’ came from).

These thoughts are due to talking to John Salvatier, but I can’t remember if that’s because he said them all or caused me to think them. I have thought about this occasionally since.

For questions such as how society should be run, I am liable to transfer them into the context of a party and think a bit about what should happen there. When I wanted to help find a name recently, we threw a naming party (which I think was where ‘Evitable’ came from).

These thoughts are due to talking to John Salvatier, but I can’t remember if that’s because he said them all or caused me to think them. I have thought about this occasionally since.

We return to Bold Monk brewing for a vigorous discussion of rationalism and whatever else we deem fit for discussion – hopefully including actual discussions of the sequences and Hamming Circles/Group Debugging.

Suite D-1

We will also do at least one proper (one person with the problem, 3 extra helper people) Hamming Circle / Group Debugging exercise.

A note on food and drink – we have used up our grant money – so we have to pay the full price of what we consume. We will be outside out front (in the breezeway) – this is subject to change, but we will be somewhere in Bold Monk. If you do not see us in the front of the restaurant, please check upstairs and out back – look for the yellow table sign. We will have to play the weather by ear. Bold Monk moved us a bit at the March Meetup, so if you don’t see us, just keep looking, or ask at the host stand.

Remember – bouncing around in conversations is a rationalist norm!

Please RSVP

items.title: When I Salsa dance, am I supposed to... try?
items.content:
I had my birthday party on a Saturday in August. After the party ended, a few of us went out to a nearby bar. Most of my family on my mom’s side is Ecuadorian[1], and my cousin from that side of the family was with us.

She was wonderfully drunk and is a natural people person who wants to meet everybody and talk to everybody, and this being eight hours into a birthday-party+bar Drinking Event, we were having random discussions about ethnicity, which somehow led to her drunkenly deciding I was 27% Latino, knighting me as such, and running around the bar informing various strangers of my new ethnic status. This led to a Latina woman inviting me to Salsa dance.

This was a disaster, because I have never enjoyed any sort of Spanish dancing of any kind; but it’s terribly rude to turn down a woman who has asked you to dance; so I agreed. Which meant I was stepping back and forth as multiple women gave me instructions at once on the Correct Steps, and which to do at what time, and at my best I only managed to sort of scoot forward at the right times and scoot backward at the right times.

And I don’t hate dancing! Especially 8 hours of birthday drinking in, I don’t typically mind dancing at all. I feel I am actually quite good at it when the right sort of music is on and I get to freestyle and dance however I feel like. The problem is that Salsa is Step Dancing. There are steps, and what it is to dance Salsa is to perform those steps. Google Search AI says that this is how you dance Salsa:

For the Leader (Starting with the Left Foot)

- Count 1: Step forward with your left foot.
- Count 2: Replace your weight in place onto your right foot.
- Count 3: Step back with your left foot (or bring your feet together).
- Count 4: Hold / pause.
- Count 5: Step backward with your right foot.
- Count 6: Replace your weight in place onto your left foot.
- Count 7: Step forward with your right foot (or bring your feet together).
- Count 8: Hold / pause....
